summary: Defines a portion of the Management Information Base for managing Traffic Engineered (TE) tunnels, such as MPLS label switched paths.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3970 defines a set of SNMP objects, a MIB module, for managing traffic-engineered tunnels, the pre-planned paths that carry traffic across a network. A management program can create a tunnel, describe the route its path should take, and then read counters for the octets and packets that have crossed it. It also defines four notifications so a manager hears when a tunnel comes up, goes down, changes path or is rerouted.

subtitle: SNMP objects for configuring and monitoring traffic-engineered tunnels such as MPLS label switched paths.

tldr.problem: A network operator had no standard way to set up and watch traffic-engineered tunnels, such as MPLS label switched paths, over SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: The MIB module adds four groups of objects: TE information, a table of tunnels, a table of the paths those tunnels take, and a table of the hops that make up a path, plus four notifications for tunnel state changes.
tldr.outcome: The module lets a management station create a tunnel, build a path hop by hop, and read back counters and state. It can only be used at the tunnel's ingress, and RFC 3970 was later updated by RFC 9141.

facts.label: Tunnel index when not an interface

today: RFC 3970 was published in January 2005 as a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 9141. The module remains the standard way to manage traffic-engineered tunnels over SNMP.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community. In particular, it describes managed objects for Traffic Engineered (TE) Tunnels, for example Multi-Protocol Label Switched Paths.

The MIB module allows one to configure TE Tunnels, to assign one or more paths to a Tunnel, and to monitor operational aspects of the Tunnel, such as the number of octets and packets that have passed through it.

As it stands, the module can only be used to configure or monitor a TE Tunnel at its ingress. The ingress is then expected to use some protocol, such as RSVP-TE, to signal the other routers in the path the information they need to set up the tunnel. Extension of the module for use at other points of a Tunnel is left for further study.
sections.plainLanguage: A traffic-engineered tunnel is a path a network operator sets up in advance so traffic follows it. This document gives SNMP objects for creating such a tunnel and for reading what it is doing. It only covers the router where the tunnel starts.

sections.title: The Internet-Standard Management Framework
sections.content: Managed objects are accessed via a virtual information store, termed the Management Information Base or MIB. MIB objects are generally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). Objects in the MIB are defined using the mechanisms defined in the Structure of Management Information (SMI). This memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant to SMIv2, which is described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580. For a detailed overview of the documents that describe the current Internet-Standard Management Framework, the memo points to section 7 of RFC 3410.
sections.plainLanguage: A MIB is a named set of counters and settings that a network device exposes. SNMP is the protocol a manager uses to read and write them, and SMIv2 is the notation used to define them.

sections.title: Overview of the MIB Module
sections.content:
The Traffic Engineering MIB module consists of four parts: Traffic Engineering information, a table of Traffic Engineering Tunnels, a table of Paths that tunnels take, and a table of Hops that make up a tunnel path. The module also has statements for minimal and full compliance. All objects are mandatory. For minimal compliance, all objects MAY be implemented read-only; for full compliance, all objects must be implemented to their stated MAX-ACCESS capabilities. Notifications are optional.

The Traffic Engineering information part contains information about the Link State Protocols used to carry TE information, the signaling protocols used to set up Traffic Tunnels, the number of Traffic Tunnels that have been configured and that are operational, and a mapping of Administrative Group numbers, called Resource Classes in RFC 2702, to names. Administrative groups are used to label links in the Traffic Engineering topology so that include and exclude constraints can be placed on Tunnel paths.

The module also relates to two other MIB modules, the Interfaces MIB and the IP Tunnel MIB. The mechanism is to assign the TE Tunnel index, teTunnelIndex, with a valid ifIndex value in ifTable. If a TE Tunnel is deemed an interface, a new interface object is created and assigned an ifIndex value in ifTable, and then a TE Tunnel object is created with teTunnelIndex set to the same value. If, and only if, a TE Tunnel is considered an interface, it may also be considered an IP tunnel when its encapsulation is IP, in which case the interface associated with the TE Tunnel should have its ifType set to tunnel(131). If a TE Tunnel is not considered an interface, its teTunnelIndex SHOULD be set to a value at least 2^24, so that it is distinct from normal interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: The module has four parts: general information about the device, the tunnels, the paths a tunnel can take, and the hops that make up a path. A tunnel can also be registered as an ordinary interface, so that the usual interface counters apply to it.

sections.title: The Tunnel Table
sections.content:
The tunnel part contains a table of Traffic Tunnels and information about each one: the Tunnel name, its configuration information, its operational information, and the active paths the Tunnel takes.

Configuration information includes the end points of the Traffic Tunnel, given as a source address type and address and a destination address type and address, and the number of configured paths for the Traffic Tunnel. The address types are typically IPv4 or IPv6, with a prefix length of 32 or 128 respectively. If the TE Tunnel path is computed by a path computation server, more flexible source address types can be used, such as AS numbers or prefix lengths shorter than a host address.

Operational information includes the current state, which is one of unknown, up, down or testing, the count of octets and packets sent on the Traffic Tunnel, how long it has been up, and how many state transitions it has had. The counters are teTunnelOctets, teTunnelPackets, teTunnelLPOctets and teTunnelLPPackets, and teTunnelDiscontinuityTimer holds the value of sysUpTime at the last time one of them jumped.

Operational path information includes the number of operational paths, the number of path changes, and when the last path change was. The tunnel name is a string of up to 32 characters and MUST be unique; a SET request that reuses a name must return an inconsistentValue error.
sections.plainLanguage: Each tunnel row holds its endpoints, its state, and counters for the octets and packets that have crossed it. The counters can jump when the device restarts, so a timestamp records when that last happened.

sections.title: Path Information
sections.content:
A Tunnel is a logical entity. An instantiation of a Tunnel is one or more Paths, and each Path has a route, also called an Explicit Route, or sequence of hops. A Path is indexed by a dual index: the primary index is that of the Tunnel to which the Path belongs, and the secondary index is that of the Path itself.

The configured information for a Path consists of the constraints for the Path and a configured route. The operational information consists of the Path status, the computed route, meaning the route that was computed to satisfy the constraints, and the actual path as recorded by the signaling protocol.

Each path row carries a type, which is one of other, primary, standby or secondary, and the constraints on the route. Those constraints are tePathIncludeAny, tePathIncludeAll and tePathExclude, each a bit vector over administrative groups, plus tePathBandwidth in kilobits per second, and the setup and hold priorities, each a value from 0 to 7 where 0 is the highest. For each link the path goes through, the link must have at least one of the groups in IncludeAny, and all of the groups in IncludeAll, and the intersection of the link's groups with the exclude set must be null.

The operational status of a path is one of unknown, down, testing, dormant, ready or operational. Down means signaling failed, dormant means the path is not signaled for a backup tunnel, ready means it is signaled but not yet carrying traffic, and operational means it is signaled and carrying traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: A path says which route to follow and what that route must satisfy. The constraints let you say, for example, that every link must belong to a certain group of links and must not belong to another one.

sections.title: Hop Information
sections.content:
A path consists of a sequence of hops. A hop can be loose, meaning that the path eventually traverses the specified node, or strict, meaning that the specified node and possibly the link must be the next node in the path. A hop can be specified as an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address, an Autonomous System number or an unnumbered interface index.

The Hop Table contains all hops for all paths on a given router. It is organized with a primary index that identifies a list of hops and a secondary index that identifies individual hops. To get the sequence of recorded hops for a path, one looks up the path's tePathRecordedRoute, which is a primary index into the Hop Table, and then uses a secondary index of 1, 2 and so on to get the actual hops in order.
sections.plainLanguage: Each hop names one node the path should pass through, and says whether the path has to go there next or may pass through it later. The hop table is a single flat list, split into numbered lists so that each path can point at its own.

sections.title: Creating, Modifying and Deleting a Tunnel
sections.content:
To create a TE Tunnel, one first obtains a free Tunnel index by using the object teNextTunnelIndex. One then creates the Tunnel, including all parameters, either as createAndGo or createAndWait. TE Paths for this Tunnel can then be created by using the teTunnelNextPathIndex object, again as createAndGo or createAndWait. A particular Path is computed and signaled when both the Path and the enclosing Tunnel have RowStatus active.

To build a Path's configured route, one first gets a free PathHop index by using teNextPathHopIndex, then builds the route hop by hop using the secondary index, setting the AddrType, Address and HopType for each Hop. Finally, one sets tePathConfiguredRoute in the Path to the PathHop index obtained.

Modifying certain properties of a TE Tunnel or a TE Path may require setting the RowStatus of the Tunnel or Path to notInService before making the changes, and then setting the RowStatus back to active to re-signal all Paths of the Tunnel or the modified Path. A TE Tunnel and all its Paths can be deleted by setting the Tunnel's RowStatus to destroy. A specific Path within a Tunnel can be destroyed by setting that Path's RowStatus to destroy.

The module defines four notifications. teTunnelUp is generated when a tunnel transitions to the up state, which happens when at least one of its paths is up. teTunnelDown is generated when the tunnel transitions to down. teTunnelChanged is generated when an active path changes or a new path becomes active. teTunnelRerouted is generated when the active path stays the same but its route changes. Each of these MUST be limited to at most one every minute, in case a tunnel flaps.
sections.plainLanguage: Building a tunnel is a sequence of steps: take a free index, create the row, add a path, add the hops of that path, then mark things active so the device computes and signals the route. Deleting is done by marking rows for destruction.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The MIB module relates to the configuration and management of Traffic Engineering tunnels. Unauthorized manipulation of fields in the tables teAdminGroupTable, teTunnelTable, tePathTable and tePathHopTable may lead to tunnel flapping, tunnel paths being changed, or traffic being disrupted. If these tables are read by unauthorized parties, the information can be used to trace traffic patterns, traffic volumes and tunnel paths, and some providers may consider this proprietary and confidential information.

Changing teAdminGroupTable affects the semantics of include and exclude constraints, so traffic takes unintended routes. Changing teTunnelTable affects many properties of traffic tunnels. Changing tePathTable affects the constraints, including bandwidth, of tunnel paths, as well as the status of the path. Changing tePathHopTable affects the route followed by a tunnel path.

Some readable objects may also be sensitive, so it is important to control even GET and NOTIFY access to them and possibly to encrypt their values when sending them over the network via SNMP. SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. It is RECOMMENDED that implementers consider the security features provided by the SNMPv3 framework, including full support for the SNMPv3 cryptographic mechanisms for authentication and privacy, and that deployment of SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who can write to these tables can reroute traffic, and anyone who can read them can learn where traffic goes and how much. The memo therefore recommends SNMPv3 with its encryption and authentication switched on.

viz.caption: THE FOUR PARTS OF THE TE MIB

items.label: dormant
items.desc: Not signaled, for a backup tunnel.

items.label: ready
items.desc: Signaled but not yet carrying traffic.

items.label: teTunnelUp
items.desc: The tunnel changed to the up state.

items.label: teTunnelDown
items.desc: The tunnel changed to the down state.

items.label: teTunnelChanged
items.desc: An active path changed or a new path became active.

items.label: teTunnelRerouted
items.desc: The active path stayed the same but its route changed.
